summary:
AstroHealth is an interactive web-based health monitoring tool designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It allows crew members to log key health indicators — heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, and mood — and instantly receive color-coded status assessments and guidance based on NASA Human Research Program (HRP) risks.

The tool features a clickable body map linked to spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation, gravity changes, etc.), trend charts over mission days, measurement instructions for non-physician crew, and a simple health score system. It addresses the challenge by enabling astronauts to self-assess their health when medical support from Earth is delayed or unavailable, supporting crew autonomy and early detection of issues related to the five hazards of human spaceflight.
details:
AstroHealth is a fully client-side web application that helps astronauts monitor and interpret their health during space missions. Users can log six key indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep hours, and mood). The system immediately classifies each reading as Nominal, Caution, or Attention Needed using spaceflight-informed thresholds and provides contextual guidance tied to NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight.

Key features include:

- Interactive body map that explains risks related to different body systems (SANS, cardiovascular deconditioning, bone/muscle loss, etc.)

- Dynamic trend charts over mission days

- Clear measurement instructions written for non-physician crew

- Environment selector (ISS, Deep Space Transit, Lunar, Mars)

- Mission Health Score and simple gamification (streaks/achievements)

The project was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Data is stored locally in the browser. Charts are powered by Chart.js. Design and clinical context were informed by NASA Human Research Program resources, including the 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight, Risks of Human Spaceflight, and Spaceflight Standard Measures.

The intended impact is to support crew self-sufficiency and early health awareness on missions where real-time support from Earth is limited.
projectRefs: Canadian Space Agency – Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health
